positiveIntegerProperty.decision: LEFT IN PLACE - it does NOT matter
positiveIntegerProperty.reason: It is #[cfg(test)] and therefore not compiled into the release binary, so it costs the hot path nothing. It also still has a live test caller, so deleting it would break the build. This was checked, not assumed.

isolation.reason: The live backtest crate DID NOT COMPILE at measurement time: `error[E0425]: cannot find value \`finding_order\` in this scope` at backtest/src/compare.rs:82. That file is owned by fidelity-developer and is mid-edit. It is not in my write set and I did not touch it.
isolation.method: robocopy byte-copy of backtest/ (excluding target/) to a scratch directory, then `git show HEAD:backtest/src/compare.rs` restored ONLY that one peer-owned file in the COPY. The live tree was not modified.
isolation.whyNotAWorktree: Only 9 of the 28 fixture directories are tracked at HEAD and one tracked fixture (comprehensive) is deleted on disk. A git worktree would have supplied 9 fixtures including the deleted one and omitted 19, shrinking the denominator in one direction while resurrecting it in the other. A byte-copy preserves the real corpus.
isolation.denominatorVerifiedInCopy: 28 fixtures / 44 mutants, counted directly in the copy and matching a direct count of the live source.

reachabilityCaveat.evidence: backtest/src/fixture.rs:244 is the ONLY use of the recreate binary and it feeds the processEvidence probe alone. The qualification loads static fixture HTML into two browsers and compares captures; it never invokes the generator, so it cannot execute fluid_height_paths.
reachabilityCaveat.meaning: The unchanged 44/44 proves GATE INTEGRITY ONLY. It is NOT evidence that this refactor is correct. The correctness claim rests entirely on the golden master below.

byteIdentity.oracle: golden master / characterization test - the correct oracle because a pure refactor is forbidden to change emitted source
byteIdentity.method: For each spec, every emitted file hashed SHA-256, entries sorted by path, joined as path=hash, and the joined manifest hashed again to one aggregate SHA-256. Both arms run 5 times.
byteIdentity.isolation: Both arms measured inside a single detached worktree at 216c24f with a private CARGO_TARGET_DIR, because peers were concurrently editing src/generate/ (jsx_app.rs, jsx_state_generation.rs, new templates/) in the live tree, which would have changed emitted output underneath both arms and voided the comparison.

endToEnd.budgetInterpretation: sum across the 5 specs, as stated in the assignment
endToEnd.verdictReason: Arm B median 13217ms and best-case min 12135ms both exceed the 5000ms budget. The hoist removes roughly half the end-to-end time but does not by itself bring the sum inside budget. Even the single fastest observed run is 2.4x the budget, so no amount of host-noise correction changes this verdict.
endToEnd.perSpecObservation: The three specs that improved are exactly the ones with large authored CSS rule sets, which is the signature the css-base-subphase profile predicted (cost scales states x nodes x rules). fluid-r5 and recreate-output are flat, correctly indicating they were never paying this cost.
endToEnd.secondaryInterpretation: If the 5000ms budget were read PER SPEC rather than as a sum, arm B would meet it at the median on all five specs (worst median 4039ms) whereas arm A missed on three (7032, 7037, 8037). The assignment says sum, so the recorded verdict is MISSED; this alternative is noted, not claimed.
endToEnd.hostContention: The host is saturated by concurrent peer browser runs; the qualification cost table itself reports host load between 100% and 287%. All timings are therefore CONTAMINATED UPPER BOUNDS. A prior control measured ~900ms of host noise on an unchanged binary. Additionally, observed wall times quantize near 1000ms boundaries, so per-run precision is roughly +/-1s and only the arm-to-arm gap (about 14s at the median) is far enough outside the noise band to be load-bearing.

negativeCase.requirement: confirm a clean result is reachable by disabling the change and seeing the failure return
negativeCase.applicability: The mutation gate CANNOT execute the changed code (see reachabilityCaveat), so disabling the change cannot make the gate fail. Reporting a gate-based negative case here would have been a false fact.
negativeCase.substituted: The reachable negative case is the timing signal itself: with the change disabled (arm A) the per-spec cost returns to 7032/7037/8037ms on the three rule-heavy specs, and with it restored (arm B) it drops to 2235/2034/3031ms. The effect disappears when disabled and returns when restored, on the same binary source, in the same worktree, counterbalanced across 5 runs each.

testSuiteControl.withChange: cargo test --release --bin recreate -> 264 passed, 1 failed, 2 ignored; failure release_gate_tests::generic_browser_release_gate, panic at src/release_gate_tests/browser_support.rs:42 'browser did not start'.
testSuiteControl.withoutChange: Same test at unmodified HEAD in the same worktree -> also FAILED, 0 passed 1 failed, panic at src/release_gate_tests/mod.rs:69 'shared Vite build failed with exit code: 1'.
testSuiteControl.conclusion: The failure is PRE-EXISTING and environmental (browser launch / Vite build on a saturated host), not caused by this change. It reproduces at unmodified HEAD. The two panic sites differ between runs, which is itself the signature of an environment-dependent failure rather than a deterministic code defect.
